title: Walking in the city
hookLine: the walk to the bus can be meditation too

cards: Tuesday, 8:12. You're late, the coffee is too hot, the bus is two blocks away and pulling in. Nobody on that sidewalk is lifting, moving and placing.

There's a horn, a dog, a man on a speakerphone. All week you've had a lane: fifteen quiet steps, a slow turn, fifteen back. It's easy to think meditation lives in the lane and the city is where it goes to die.
So does the walk to the bus count too? The old texts give a generous answer.

teach.h: THE LANE IS TRAINING, NOT THE GAME.
teach.b: The lane is a training ground, not the whole game. In the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, the Buddha describes a practitioner who knows the body in every posture.
When walking, they know they're walking. Standing, sitting, lying down: the same. Then the text goes further.
Going out and coming back, looking ahead and looking away, bending and stretching, eating, drinking, even using the toilet: all of it can be done with clear knowing.

The word for that is sampajanna, clear comprehension: you know what you're doing while you're doing it, and why. Nothing in that list requires a quiet lane. So a city walk is a real practice, just a different one.
In the lane you slow everything down.

teach.h: NORMAL PACE, EYES OPEN, FEET FIRST.
teach.b: On the sidewalk you walk at a normal pace, eyes open, watching for traffic, because clear knowing includes knowing the curb is there. What you bring is the thread: the feel of the feet. Heel, sole, toes.
When the mind jumps to the meeting or the argument you're rehearsing, notice it and come back to the feet.

teach.h: A RED LIGHT AS A BELL.
teach.b: Some teachers use the city itself as the bell. Thich Nhat Hanh, the Vietnamese Zen teacher, suggested treating a red light or a ringing phone as a small call home to the breath.

You're stopped anyway; you might as well arrive. So the walk to the bus isn't wasted time between sessions. For someone with a job and kids and a commute, it may be most of the practice there's time for.
The feet are always with you.

how: Some Buddhist teachers encourage walking practice outside the retreat lane: on the way to work, in a parking lot, at a stoplight, simply knowing the body is walking while walking at a normal pace.

o: emptying the mind of every last thought
knowing what you're doing while you do it
a loud bell rung to start the day

games.q: match the piece to what it means on a city walk.
p: a training ground, slow and quiet
clear knowing: what you're doing, and why
the thread you come back to
a bell the city rings for you

s: walking meditation only counts if you walk very slowly
in the city you walk at a normal pace; the practice is knowing you're walking.
the old text lists eating, drinking and even the toilet as times for clear knowing
the discourse on mindfulness includes all of those, not just the meditation hall.
mindful walking means closing your eyes to go inward
eyes stay open: clear knowing includes knowing where the curb is.

games.q: you're on the sidewalk, rehearsing an argument with your boss. you notice. what now?
o: stop walking until the thought is gone.
notice it, and come back to the feet.
give up: the city is too loud to practice.
games.why: that's the whole practice: notice where the mind went, and return to the feel of the feet. you keep walking the whole time.

practice: Stand up if you can, feel the floor under both feet, and walk a few steps at your ordinary speed, feeling each foot land: heel, sole, toes. Stop, stand, and let the breath come and go.
Then sit and picture tomorrow's first real walk, the door, the street, the corner, and pick one spot on that route, a crosswalk or a stoplight, to be your bell.

wordCard.voice: Sampajanna. Clear comprehension, knowing what you're doing while you do it: walking in the city, at a normal pace, eyes open, the feet as the thread.

orig.note: Pali: clear comprehension, knowing what you're doing while you do it; paired with sati, mindfulness.

carryVoice: Your line: every step, here. Even a red light can be a bell. Day one hundred twenty-one, complete.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 (Satipatthana Sutta), the postures and clear comprehension
Thich Nhat Hanh, teaching on red lights and ringing phones as bells of mindfulness
